The Golden-crowned spadebill (Platyrinchus coronatus) is a small Neotropical passerine that exhibits a remarkably rapid developmental trajectory, a pattern likely shaped by the high predation pressure typical of its understory forest habitat. Females construct a compact cup nest into which they deposit a clutch of two to three eggs [N_R_i = nest into which they deposit a clutch of two to three eggs], and field observations consistently indicate that a single brood is raised per breeding season [F_R_i = single brood is raised per breeding season]. These eggs are incubated at approximately 35 °C [T = 35 °C], and under these thermal conditions the nestlings hatch after an incubation period of roughly 12 days [ab = roughly 12 days]. The newly hatched young are altricial, weighing just 1.2 grams [Wwb = 1.2 grams] at the moment of emergence, a minimal investment that is characteristic of many tyrannid flycatchers and which necessitates an intense period of biparental provisioning immediately following the first exogenous feeding event.

Once the nestlings have successfully hatched, the subsequent developmental period proceeds with notable speed when considered within the broader context of the Tyrannidae family. Under the consistent thermal conditions associated with the species' active metabolic range (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a particularly striking metric of this rapid pace is the timing of fledging: young birds depart the nest approximately 12 days after hatching [tx = approximately 12 days after hatching]. This brief nestling phase is substantially shorter than that observed in several related tyrannids of comparable adult body mass, suggesting an adaptive strategy to minimize exposure to nest predators. Following fledging, the chicks remain dependent on their parents for an additional period while they refine their flight skills and foraging techniques, culminating in a transition to nutritional independence that marks the end of the parental-fed chick stage and the beginning of a pre-reproductive juvenile phase in the dense forest understory.

The transition from the juvenile stage to a sexually mature adult is also compressed in this species, a life-history feature that may reflect the relatively high extrinsic mortality rates in its environment. Evidence from captive-reared individuals indicates that gonadal maturation is completed quite early, with puberty attained at approximately 36 days after hatching [tp = approximately 36 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at a body temperat at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]ure of 40.2 °C. However, the onset of actual reproductive activity does not coincide precisely with the achievement of sexual maturity. The first successful breeding event, or first brood, is typically deferred until an individual reaches about 365 days after hatching [tR = about 365 days after hatching], also measured at this same body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This one-year delay between reaching puberty and engaging in reproduction is a common pattern among small Neotropical passerines, and it is often linked to the time required for a young bird to establish a territory and acquire the necessary foraging experience within a competitive forest matrix.

Adult females of this species ultimately attain a stable body mass of approximately 11 grams [Wwi = approximately 11 grams], a figure that represents the maximum wet weight typically recorded for reproductively active individuals. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the general allometric scaling relationships observed across the Tyrannidae. While some museum compilations, such as those from Avibase, have listed a slightly lower mean mass of 9.15 grams for this species, the higher value aligns more closely with the energetic demands imposed by a metabolic rate of 29.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 29.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour], measured at the standard body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption rate is a critical physiological baseline that supports the high activity levels required for aerial insectivory in the humid lowland forests of Central and South America where the Golden-crowned spadebill is resident.

Despite its rapid early development and early sexual maturation, the species is not particularly long-lived, a trade-off that is common among small-bodied passerines facing high predation rates. Under natural thermal conditions averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for the Golden-crowned spadebill is approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days], a longevity calculated from mark-recapture studies of individuals. This translates to roughly seven years of age, a duration that represents a relatively short window for reproductive contribution, especially given that the first reproduction event usually occurs at the beginning of the second year. The species thus relies on a high intrinsic rate of increase to maintain stable populations, a demographic strategy that is complemented by the repeated production of clutches containing two to five eggs per year [Ri = two to five eggs per year] across the limited number of breeding opportunities available during its adult life.
